Details: Describes the current starter implementation, operational workflows, recommended skills, technical choices, alternatives, and glossary.

Implemented means the code path exists. Email-provider registration, database provisioning, API credentials, GitHub repository setup, and deployment secrets still need environment-specific configuration.

Email-driven incident and alert triage application: accepts alerts from multiple locations, assigns P1-P4 priority and response SLA, stores original email and incident lifecycle in PostgreSQL, and provides a daily queue, backlog, and AI assistant for alerts and operational knowledge.
The inbound endpoint is ready for a mail provider; live knowledge connectors require credentials; dashboard falls back to sample data when PostgreSQL is unavailable.
An email system or forwarding service parses an inbound message and calls POST /api/alerts/intake with a bearer token.
The API checks the token, validates required fields and size limits, and rejects duplicate messageId values.
A keyword classifier assigns P1, P2, P3, or P4. Initial response targets: P1 = 30 minutes; P2 = 60 minutes; P3 = 240 minutes; P4 = 480 minutes.
PostgreSQL stores the original message, text and HTML bodies, sender, recipient, location, priority, SLA, status, and creation time. An activity event records receipt.
The alert appears in the daily dashboard or backlog based on creation date, current Eastern time, and status.
Classification rules are a starting point, not a trained model or configurable policy engine. Review and tune them against organizational incident policy before production.
Before 5:00 PM in America/New_York, the dashboard shows all alerts created on the current Eastern calendar date, regardless of whether they are Open, In progress, or Resolved.
At or after 5:00 PM Eastern, the daily dashboard closes and shows no alerts for that day.
Open and In progress alerts from earlier Eastern dates appear in Backlog. After cutoff, unresolved alerts from the current date also move into Backlog.
Resolved alerts from earlier dates are excluded from Backlog; resolved alerts from today remain on the dashboard until its cutoff.
An alert created after the cutoff is placed in Backlog while the daily dashboard is closed.
Backlog is a computed view; it does not change the alert database status to a separate Backlog state.

The code uses IANA zone America/New_York, which observes daylight saving time. 5 PM ET means 5 PM local Eastern time, not a permanently fixed UTC-5 offset. The browser refreshes alert lists every 30 seconds.
Operators can create an alert from the dashboard. With a configured database, POST /api/alerts stores it.
Assignment and status actions call PATCH /api/alerts/{reference} and add activity records.
Resolving an alert sets its close time; starting work records its first-response time.
In sample mode, manual changes exist only in browser memory.
The dashboard sends the operator question and selected model provider to POST /api/assistant.
When a database is configured, the server gathers active-alert context and relevant indexed KnowledgeDocument records from PostgreSQL.
The server also searches configured SharePoint, Jira, and Confluence connectors.
The server sends context to OpenAI API or Anthropic API and returns the answer. Provider keys stay on the server.

Database retrieval ranks records with simple keyword matching. SharePoint, Jira, and Confluence are live search adapters. There is no completed scheduled synchronization/indexing pipeline, vector database, semantic embedding search, or full RAG pipeline. Coverage and answer quality depend on provider permissions and search results.
Email provider, operator browser, Next.js APIs, PostgreSQL via Prisma, SharePoint, Jira, Confluence, OpenAI or Anthropic, GitHub Actions, and Vercel UAT/production promotion.

Details: Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, and CSS fit the existing project and provide typed UI plus server routes in one deployment.
Vite + React is lighter for a standalone SPA but needs a separate API service. Vue/Svelte are viable but would be a rewrite.
Next.js route handlers on Node.js form a modular monolith that keeps alert APIs, assistant calls, and UI close together and avoids early service-to-service operations.

FastAPI/Python suits Python-first teams or substantial ML/data processing but adds a second service and deployment. Express/Fastify are options for a separate Node API but duplicate some Next.js capability.
PostgreSQL provides durable alert, email, activity, and knowledge metadata storage. ACID transactions and mature indexing suit incident records.
Managed PostgreSQL is a deployment alternative, not a different data model. MongoDB is less natural for relational lifecycle records.
Prisma ORM provides a schema, generated TypeScript client, and migrations.
Drizzle or Kysely are lighter TypeScript-first SQL options. SQLAlchemy fits a Python/FastAPI backend. Raw SQL gives control but requires more mapping and maintenance.
Authenticated HTTPS webhook allows a mail provider to forward parsed fields while keeping provider-specific parsing outside the app.
Microsoft Graph subscriptions, Gmail API, SES inbound, or mailbox polling can be added when a provider is chosen. Direct IMAP polling is more operationally fragile.
A small keyword-based rule set makes the starter usable and inspectable.
A configurable rule engine improves policy management. ML/LLM classification may help later but needs evaluation, guardrails, and human review for critical alerts.
OpenAI or Anthropic server APIs are selected per request; keys remain server-side.
Azure OpenAI or an enterprise-hosted model may meet organization-specific governance needs. A provider abstraction is advisable if models proliferate.
Server-side live API search uses Microsoft Graph and Atlassian REST APIs and keeps vendor access and credentials out of the browser.
Scheduled ingestion into a search index improves cross-source retrieval and auditability but adds sync jobs, permission management, and stale-data handling.
Keyword matching against selected database records plus provider-native searches keeps starter infrastructure overhead low.
PostgreSQL full-text search or pgvector embeddings improve relevance at additional indexing and evaluation cost.
GitHub Actions provides verification/promotion and Vercel hosts Next.js.
Azure App Service/Container Apps, AWS, or another Node-capable host can be used. Match the host to database, identity, networking, and compliance requirements.
One modular application and PostgreSQL database; current scope does not require microservices.

Add a background worker for slow or retryable email parsing or knowledge sync when needed. Split into independently deployed services only when scaling, ownership, isolation, or availability justify distributed-system overhead.

Add tests for Eastern-time boundaries, duplicate email delivery, priority rules, permissions, and database migrations.
Decide whether to implement knowledge synchronization, permission-aware indexing, audit/retention rules, and semantic retrieval.
Add observability, backups, alerting on failed email ingestion, rate limits, and LLM cost controls.
Severity definitions, response/resolve SLAs, escalation paths, ownership, on-call workflows, and audit requirements.
React, TypeScript, Next.js App Router, forms, accessible interaction, responsive CSS, and client/server boundaries.

MIME structure, parsing, webhook delivery, retries, duplicate detection, sender validation, and treating inbound content as untrusted.

LLM APIs, context construction, retrieval quality, prompt-injection defense, citations, evaluation, privacy, and token/cost limits.
Secret management, TLS, authentication, least privilege, data retention, audit trails, and secure handling of email and incident content.
Git branching, GitHub Actions, environment secrets, CI gates, database migrations, Vercel deployments, rollback, and release approvals.
Unit and integration tests, API contract tests, timezone/DST boundary tests, accessibility checks, and end-to-end workflows.
A small team can combine responsibilities, but incident policy, access control, and production release ownership should have named reviewers.

Server-side code that validates requests, applies rules, accesses data, and calls external providers.
A secret sent in an HTTP Authorization header; possession grants the permissions associated with that token.
Code running in the user's browser. Provider secrets must not be placed here.
A URL path and HTTP method handled by the server, such as POST /api/alerts/intake.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol; HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS encryption.
JavaScript Object Notation, a common structured data format for API requests and responses.
React framework used here for the browser application and Node.js server routes.
JavaScript runtime used to run the app server and development/build tools; it is not itself a browser UI framework.
Node Package Manager; installs project dependencies and runs scripts declared in package.json.
npm tool that runs a package executable, such as npx prisma generate.
JavaScript/TypeScript library used to build the interactive user interface.
Representational State Transfer, a common HTTP API style using resources and methods such as GET, POST, and PATCH.
Next.js server function that implements an HTTP endpoint.
JavaScript with static types; TSX allows JSX markup inside TypeScript React files.
An HTTP request one system sends to another when an event occurs. Here it is the planned email-to-alert delivery mechanism.
Computed view of unresolved alerts carried over from previous Eastern dates, plus unresolved alerts after the daily cutoff. It is not a separate alert status in PostgreSQL.
Daily dashboard close at 5:00 PM America/New_York.
Local civil time in the U.S. Eastern zone. The project uses America/New_York, so it switches between EST (UTC-5) and EDT (UTC-4) for daylight saving time.
Fixed UTC-5 standard-time offset. Everyday speech often uses EST year-round; the code uses America/New_York for correct seasonal wall-clock behavior.
Prevents a retry of the same message from creating a second alert. Current intake uses unique messageId values when the provider supplies them.
Project priority levels. P1 is highest; P4 is lowest. Classification policy must be agreed with the operations team.
Service Level Agreement: target time for response or resolution. This starter stores a response target in minutes but does not implement contractual pause calendars or escalation automation.
Lifecycle state OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, or RESOLVED. A resolved alert remains on today's dashboard until cutoff.
Database transaction properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.
Create, read, update, and delete, the basic data operations. This starter supports alert creation, reading, and updates; it does not provide alert deletion in the UI.
Database constraint connecting a record to its parent, such as an activity event to its alert.
Database structure that speeds up selected searches and sorts at the cost of storage and write work.
Versioned database change applied in a controlled sequence. prisma migrate dev is for local development; prisma migrate deploy applies checked-in migrations in deployment environments.
Object-Relational Mapper: library that maps application objects to relational database operations.
Relational database storing alerts, original email content, activity events, and knowledge metadata.

The ORM used by this project. prisma/schema.prisma describes database models; Prisma CLI generates the TypeScript client and manages migrations; @prisma/client is the generated runtime library used by application code.
Unique database identifier for a row.
Definition of database tables/models, columns, types, relations, and constraints.
Database rule preventing duplicate values, such as repeated message IDs.
Company providing Jira and Confluence, used here as external knowledge sources.

HTTP authentication scheme sending a username/password pair encoded in a header. It is not encryption by itself and must only be used over HTTPS; replace the starter shared-password gate with SSO for broad production use.

Server-side adapter that translates Synopse search into a vendor API request and maps the response into a common result format. It is not live until credentials, permissions, and endpoint configuration are provided.
Microsoft identity platform formerly branded Azure Active Directory; can issue application tokens for Microsoft Graph.
Large Language Model: AI model that produces text from instructions and context. This project can call OpenAI or Anthropic models.
Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions: standard format for email headers, body types, and attachments. rawEmail is retained for audit; text and html are parsed representations.
Microsoft API used by the SharePoint connector to search permitted content.
Server-to-server authentication flow in which an application uses tenant, client ID, and secret to obtain a short-lived access token.
Untrusted text in an email or document attempting to change AI model instructions. The assistant prompt tells the model to treat retrieved content as data; this is mitigation, not a guarantee.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant source material and supply it to an LLM. Synopse has basic keyword retrieval and live provider searches; it does not yet have a full vector-based RAG/indexing pipeline.
Regular expression: pattern language for finding text matches. Initial priority classifier uses regex patterns for terms such as P1, critical, or service unavailable.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, standard protocol for sending email. The starter does not run an SMTP server; an email platform must forward messages to its webhook.
In AI usage, a unit of text processed by a model; in authentication, a credential. Meaning depends on context.
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery or Deployment: automation that checks code and can deploy it after defined gates. GitHub Actions provides these workflows here.
Command-Line Interface: program operated by typed terminal commands, for example npm, npx, prisma, or git.
Configuration value supplied to a process at runtime, commonly used for database URLs and provider credentials.

npm install requires Node.js/npm. winget can install Node.js on Windows, but it is a workstation setup tool, not part of the application.
Install PostgreSQL for Windows using the installer linked from the official PostgreSQL download page. The database server and command-line tools are required; Stack Builder add-ons are optional.
Use PostgreSQL's default local port 5432 unless another service is using it.
Confirm the server accepts local connections with pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432.

Create a login role and database named synopse, or use matching names in DATABASE_URL. Prefer lowercase role name; quoted mixed-case PostgreSQL role names are case-sensitive and must match the URL exactly.
The database role password is separate from the postgres administrator password and pgAdmin master password. pgAdmin does not display saved passwords when reopening role properties.

The role must be able to log in. prisma migrate dev may need permission to create a shadow database; grant CREATEDB locally or provision a shadow database. Do not use a superuser for normal application access.
Copy .env.example to .env, set DATABASE_URL to postgresql://synopse:<URL_ENCODED_PASSWORD>@localhost:5432/synopse?schema=public, and keep .env out of Git. The .env file is ignored by Git.
URL-encode reserved password characters, for example # as %23 and @ as %40. Do not put pgAdmin's master password in DATABASE_URL.

In local development, leave SYNOPSE_ACCESS_USER and SYNOPSE_ACCESS_PASSWORD empty to bypass starter Basic Auth. If both are set, middleware requests Basic Auth even in development. Production requires strong values for both.
If PowerShell blocks npm.ps1 because scripts are disabled, use npm.cmd and npx.cmd rather than changing machine-wide execution policy. Example: npm.cmd run db:migrate.

If migration output says the migration was applied and database is in sync but Prisma then reports EPERM renaming query_engine-windows.dll.node, the migration succeeded and later client-engine replacement was blocked by a file lock. Stop Next.js dev server and other Node/Prisma processes, run npm.cmd run db:generate, then restart npm.cmd run dev. Do not rerun the migration solely to fix the DLL replacement error.
Run npm.cmd run db:seed after migrations to add eight mock alerts. The seed is idempotent by alert reference and writes PostgreSQL rows used by the dashboard.
prisma/demo-alerts.json is used by both the browser fallback and prisma/seed.cjs, keeping sample data consistent.
